content: Screening hysteroscopy in women with unexplained infertility or those preparing for intrauterine insemination (IUI) or in vitro fertilization (IVF) can identify intrauterine abnormalities that may not be detected through routine transvaginal ultrasound. Both diagnostic and operative hysteroscopy have the potential to enhance reproductive outcomes. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of screening hysteroscopy in subfertile women undergoing infertility evaluation, as well as in those preparing for IUI or IVF. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL CRSO, MEDLINE, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, with the last search performed in September 2018. Relevant articles and conference proceedings were also reviewed. Randomized controlled trials comparing screening hysteroscopy to no intervention in subfertile women attempting spontaneous conception or preparing for IUI or IVF were included. Data collection involved independent screening of studies, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment. The primary outcomes were live birth rates and complications following hysteroscopy. Data were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) and a fixed-effect model, and the quality of evidence was assessed using GRADE criteria. A total of 11 studies were identified. One trial specifically evaluated screening hysteroscopy versus no hysteroscopy in women with unexplained subfertility attempting spontaneous conception. The evidence was of very low quality, and it remains uncertain whether screening hysteroscopy improves ongoing pregnancy rates in women with at least two years of unexplained subfertility (RR 4.30, 95% CI 2.29 to 8.07; 1 RCT; 200 participants). For a clinic with a baseline ongoing pregnancy rate of 10%, screening hysteroscopy could potentially increase this rate to between 23% and 81%. No adverse events were reported in either treatment group. Similarly, it is uncertain whether clinical pregnancy rates improve (RR 3.80, 95% CI 2.31 to 6.24; 1 RCT; 200 participants) or miscarriage rates increase (RR 2.80, 95% CI 1.05 to 7.48; 1 RCT; 200 participants) following screening hysteroscopy in this population. Ten trials involving 1836 women who underwent screening hysteroscopy and 1914 women who did not undergo hysteroscopy prior to IVF were included. The quality of evidence was limited by inadequate reporting of study methods and significant statistical heterogeneity. Eight of the ten trials had unclear risk of bias regarding allocation concealment. Screening hysteroscopy before IVF may increase live birth rates (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.43; 6 RCTs; 2745 participants; I² = 69%; low-quality evidence). For a clinic with a baseline live birth rate of 22%, screening hysteroscopy could increase live birth rates to between 25% and 32%. However, sensitivity analysis of trials with a low risk of bias showed no significant increase in live birth rates (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.18; 2 RCTs; 1452 participants; I² = 0%). Only four trials reported complications following hysteroscopy, and three of these recorded no adverse events in either group. It remains uncertain whether screening hysteroscopy is associated with a higher risk of adverse events (Peto odds ratio 7.47, 95% CI 0.15 to 376.42; 4 RCTs; 1872 participants; very low-quality evidence). Screening hysteroscopy before IVF may increase clinical pregnancy rates (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.20 to 1.45; 10 RCTs; 3750 participants; I² = 49%; low-quality evidence). For a clinic with a baseline clinical pregnancy rate of 28%, screening hysteroscopy could increase clinical pregnancy rates to between 33% and 40%. There appears to be little or no difference in miscarriage rates following screening hysteroscopy (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.50; 3 RCTs; 1669 participants; I² = 0%; low-quality evidence). No trials were identified that compared screening hysteroscopy to no hysteroscopy prior to IUI. In conclusion, there is currently no high-quality evidence to support the routine use of hysteroscopy as a screening tool in subfertile women with normal findings on ultrasound or hysterosalpingogram during basic fertility evaluations. In women undergoing IVF, low-quality evidence suggests that screening hysteroscopy may improve live birth and clinical pregnancy rates. However, pooled results from the only two trials with a low risk of bias did not demonstrate a benefit of screening hysteroscopy before IVF. Given that the studies showing an effect had unclear allocation concealment, it remains uncertain whether routine screening hysteroscopy improves live birth and clinical pregnancy rates, either in the general population or in women with two or more failed IVF attempts. There is insufficient data to draw definitive conclusions about the safety of screening hysteroscopy.
